opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's a lovely example of something philosophers and psychologists have been arguing about for a very long time, which is how much of our thinking actually depends on having these picture-like representations in our heads. There was the whole imagery debate back in the seventies and eighties, with Stephen Kosslyn on one side saying images are genuinely quasi-pictorial and Zenon Pylyshyn on the other saying, no, it's all propositional underneath, and the pictures are a kind of epiphenomenal gloss.

What aphantasia suggests, I think, is that the experience of imagery and the functional capacity that imagery is supposed to support can come apart quite dramatically. You have people who say, quite sincerely, that when they try to picture their kitchen there's just nothing there, no picture at all. And yet if you ask them how many windows are in the kitchen, or which way the door opens, they can tell you perfectly well. They can do mental rotation tasks, they can navigate, they can plan. So whatever is doing the cognitive work doesn't seem to require that vivid phenomenology.

That fits with something I've been interested in for a long time, which is that our introspective access to our own minds is surprisingly poor. Some of my early work with children was about how they come to understand their own mental states, and one of the striking things is that even adults are often confabulating when they report what's going on in their heads. Aphantasia is a nice case where people discovered, sometimes in their thirties or forties, that when everyone else said "picture a sunset" they meant it literally, and they had assumed it was just a figure of speech. That tells you how little we actually compare notes on inner experience, and how much variation there might be underneath shared language.

And there's a broader lesson about variability. We tend to talk about "the human mind" as if there were one, but there's enormous individual difference in things like imagery, inner speech, even how people experience time. Some of that variation may be really functionally important, and some of it may be more like differences in the user interface, while the underlying computation is quite similar. Figuring out which is which is one of the really interesting open questions.

r001.rationale: The response says people with aphantasia may have no picture-like imagery while still performing tasks, but it does not say they vividly experience the visual world.

r002.rationale: It says imagery experience can come apart from the cognitive capacities it is supposed to support and that cognitive work does not seem to require vivid imagery, presenting imagery as unnecessary to solving tasks.

r003.rationale: The response discusses introspective access and variation in inner experience, but expresses no doubt about whether aphantasia bears on consciousness as ordinarily experienced.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think aphantasia is one of those wonderful cases where a fairly rare condition tells you something about how much we've been over-reading introspection. For a long time, going back to Galton really, psychologists assumed that when people said "I see it in my mind's eye," that was a literal description of a representational format, and that imagery was doing a lot of the heavy lifting in thought. And then you find people, perhaps two or three percent of the population, who report no imagery at all, and they're architects, they're novelists, they're perfectly capable of answering questions like "how many windows are in your house?" They just do it differently, or at least they describe doing it differently.

So the first lesson is that whatever imagery is, it's not necessary for a great deal of spatial and memory cognition that we might have thought depended on it. That doesn't mean imagery is epiphenomenal. There's decent evidence that aphantasics have somewhat different autobiographical memory, somewhat less vivid recollection of their own past, and some differences in things like fear responses to imagined scenarios. So it seems to play a role in the richness and the emotional texture of certain kinds of thought more than in the computational core of it.

The second lesson, which is the one I care about more, is a developmental one. We really don't know what the inner lives of young children are like, and the aphantasia work is a reminder that adults vary enormously in phenomenology while behaving quite similarly. My suspicion is that children's consciousness is more like a lantern than a spotlight, as I've argued, more diffuse, less controlled, and imagery in the adult sense may be partly a product of the top-down, executive control that develops over childhood. So whether a four-year-old has "mental imagery" might not even be a well-formed question in the way it is for an adult.

And the third thing is just methodological humility. The whole field of imagery rested for decades on self-report, and here's a population that shows self-report and underlying mechanism can come apart in surprising ways. That should make us careful about a lot of other claims we make from the armchair, including, I'd say, claims about what large language models do or don't "experience."

r001.rationale: The response says people with aphantasia report no imagery and can perform spatial and memory tasks; it does not say they vividly experience the visual world.

r002.rationale: The response explicitly says imagery is not necessarily epiphenomenal and may shape thought’s richness and emotional texture. It does not characterize consciously generating images during problem-solving as epiphenomenal.

r003.rationale: The response treats aphantasia as relevant to phenomenology and children’s consciousness, rather than expressing doubt that it bears on consciousness as ordinarily experienced.

astra-6.text:
I think it suggests that we should be very cautious about identifying thinking with the particular way thinking feels to us. If you have vivid visual imagery, it’s very natural to suppose that when you remember something or imagine what might happen, the picture is doing the work. And yet there are people who report no visual imagery who can still remember, reason spatially, and imagine possibilities.

That doesn’t mean imagery does nothing. It may make a difference to how you solve a problem, or to the emotional character of a memory. But having a conscious picture and having a representation that lets you reason about the world seem to be different things.

What I find particularly interesting is that people can go for years without realizing that their experience is different from other people’s. We all say, “Imagine your mother’s face,” and assume we mean the same thing. It turns out that even in this very ordinary case, our access to what’s going on in somebody else’s mind is quite limited.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes conscious pictures from representations used for reasoning, but allows imagery may affect problem-solving rather than calling it epiphenomenal.

r003.rationale: The response discusses limits of introspective access, but does not express doubt that aphantasia bears on consciousness as ordinarily experienced.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it reveals that there are more ways of thinking than we tend to suppose. If you have vivid mental imagery, it seems almost inconceivable that someone could think about their house, or remember a holiday, without having a picture in their head. Yet people with aphantasia can do many of those things perfectly well.

That suggests we should distinguish the information that a cognitive system is using from the conscious experience that accompanies it. You might represent spatial relationships without experiencing a picture. And conversely, having a very vivid picture doesn’t necessarily mean that you have a particularly accurate representation.

The developmental question I find interesting is how those different ways of representing the world emerge. Do children start out with different kinds of imagery, or do they develop different strategies? Aphantasia gives us a way of asking those questions. It also reminds us how little access we have to other people’s experience. We can agree about what’s in the world while having rather different experiences of thinking about it.

r001.rationale: The response says people with aphantasia can think about places and remember events without a mental picture, but does not say they can vividly experience the visual world.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes cognitive information from accompanying conscious experience, but does not state that consciously generating images during problem-solving is epiphenomenal or separate from the mechanism of solving.

r003.rationale: The response notes limited access to other people’s experiences, but does not express doubt that aphantasia bears on consciousness as ordinarily experienced.
